I dwell on how I used to be before the event
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a patient whose index trauma is witnessing domestic violence in childhood, sexual-trauma-specific trigger content is a poor fit unless sexual violence was part of the witnessed events. Nothing else in the profile links the trauma memory or threat meanings to sexual content, so this item is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

Avoiding sex is similarly trauma-content-specific and is not supported by the rest of the trigger, threat, or memory items for witnessed childhood domestic violence. In combination with the sexual-trauma trigger item, it suggests a different trauma theme than the one provided, making the profile clinically incoherent.

vignette:
Omar, a 41-year-old construction worker, presents as a man holding himself with a taught stillness, as if braced for an impact that never comes. For over three decades, he has carried the memory of one night in his childhood home. He speaks of it haltingly, not as a continuous story, but as a collection of stark, silent images. When he tries to deliberately piece together the sequence of events, the narrative dissolves, but the images themselves intrude with brutal clarity. He sees the floral pattern on the wallpaper behind his mother’s head, the precise moment a table lamp tipped over, its shade askew, and the splintered wood of the doorframe his father’s fist had struck. For Omar, remembering is not like replaying a film, but like being forced to look at a set of dreadful photographs he can never put away. Between these vivid snapshots are complete blanks; he has no memory of the sounds, only the shouting that came before and the ringing silence that followed.

This fragmented memory has cast a long shadow over his adult life. On the job site, a loud, sudden confrontation between two colleagues over a misplaced tool can send a jolt through his body. His heart begins to pound in his chest, a cold sweat breaks out on his neck, and he feels an urgent need to get away. Over the years, he has learned to preemptively manage this by making himself as small as possible. He avoids any situation that might lead to disagreement, never questioning the foreman’s instructions even when he spots a potential problem, and eating his lunch alone in his truck rather than joining the others. This has had tangible consequences; he was recently passed over for a promotion to crew chief, a role he knew he was qualified for, because his boss told him he needed to be more assertive.

Omar has come to believe the world is a place of hidden threats, and he is in a constant state of vigilance. He spends his days scanning the faces and body language of his coworkers, trying to decipher their moods and anticipate any sudden flare-ups of anger. A foreman’s furrowed brow or a tense set of shoulders is enough to put him on high alert for the rest of the day. This hypervigilance extends beyond people. When the concrete truck is delayed by an hour, his mind doesn’t default to traffic; instead, he becomes certain something terrible has happened—an accident, a catastrophic failure at the plant—and that the fallout will inevitably cascade down to him. The police are a particularly potent trigger. The sight of a patrol car cruising past the construction site, its presence official and unreadable, brings back the image of two uniformed officers standing in his childhood doorway, their authority feeling both immense and utterly useless.

To cope with the constant tension, Omar often retreats inward. He finds himself drifting off into a world of his own, staring blankly at a half-finished wall, his mind a quiet, empty space. He can lose minutes this way, only to be startled back to the present by a coworker calling his name. In the evenings, alone in his apartment, his thoughts turn not to fantasy but to the past. He dwells on the man he was in his twenties, before the vigilance became so exhausting—a man who could go on dates, speak his mind, and believe in a future that wasn't menacing. Now, any conversation about the future, whether it’s a simple question about his plans for the weekend or a discussion about long-term career goals, feels impossible. He cannot picture a future that is safe. He decided to seek therapy after his foreman pulled him aside to discuss his "drifting" and his reluctance to take on more responsibility. The conversation was calm, but for Omar, it was a confrontation he couldn't escape. He is here because the world he has built to protect himself has become a prison, and he is terrified he will lose his job, the last piece of solid ground beneath his feet.
